Our Mission

The Presidential Cluster on Breaking the Neural Code supports research and teaching on the neural codes underlying mental states, beliefs, experiences, and behavior. Understanding the brain at this level can help address problems such as decision-making about global challenges and improving mental and brain health.

Doing this requires new, multidisciplinary technologies and approaches that cross traditional boundaries between fields.

Home / Mission and Goals

Our Mission

Mission and Goals

Why the cluster exists, what it's working toward, and the five goals guiding its work at Dartmouth.

The Presidential Cluster on Breaking the Neural Code supports research and teaching on the neural codes underlying mental states, beliefs, experiences, and behavior. Understanding the brain at this level can help address problems such as decision-making about the environment and other global issues, and mental and brain health.

Getting there is not a single-lab or single-discipline effort. Breaking the neural code will require new, multidisciplinary technologies and approaches that cross traditional boundaries between fields of study: pairing human neuroimaging with circuit-level animal-model neuroscience, and both with the computational tools needed to make sense of increasingly large and complex data.

Computational approaches are used to understand brain organization, to develop models of the brain processes underlying human feelings and cognitive performance, and to develop translational applications for clinical use.

The cluster's activities build on existing strengths in neuroscience at Dartmouth College and aim to support a research and teaching community that continues beyond any single grant, paper, or hire.

Current Goals

Five priorities guiding the cluster's work.

  1. 01

    Faculty Hires

    Supporting hires who bring cutting-edge multidisciplinary computational and biological techniques to Dartmouth. An active search is underway to fill a third endowed faculty position bridging computational and systems neuroscience, further strengthening ties between human neuroimaging and animal-model circuit research.

  2. 02

    Enhance Research on the Neural Code

    Providing seed funding for multidisciplinary, exploratory collaborations so they can become externally competitive for larger grants and awards.

  3. 03

    Visitors & Speakers

    Bringing cutting-edge researchers to campus to share their work and to facilitate new collaborations beyond Dartmouth.

  4. 04

    Building Community

    Enhancing the physical and intellectual environment to foster cross-disciplinary communication among psychology, neuroscience, biology, computer science, engineering, cognitive science, biostatistics, and medicine around computational neuroscience.

  5. 05

    Undergraduate & Graduate Education

    Supporting and incentivizing new courses in neuroscience that align with the cluster's mission, at both the undergraduate and graduate level.

Breaking the Neural Code is one of Dartmouth's Presidential Academic Clusters, a College-wide initiative that concentrates strategic investment in faculty hiring and research infrastructure around emerging, cross-disciplinary scientific opportunities. Learn more about the Academic Clusters initiative ↗ from Dartmouth's Office of the Provost.

Priority Research Areas

Priority Research Areas

Priority Area 01

Human Computation and Behavior

Human neuroimaging, particularly fMRI and MEG, is used to study human thought, experience, and behavior. This area combines those signals with computational methods, including pattern recognition, dynamic-systems modeling, large-scale data resources, and neuromodulation, to model how the brain gives rise to feelings and cognitive performance.

  • fMRI + pattern recognition and dynamic-systems models of brain states
  • Big-data resources and large-scale computing
  • Advanced modeling of brain–behavior interrelationships
  • Neuroimaging combined with neuromodulation and multimodal recording
Explore this area Priority Area 02

Neural Population Coding and Circuits

This area studies neural circuits and how populations of neurons encode behavior. It develops and applies tools for tagging, imaging, and manipulating neural ensembles tied to behavioral states, along with the theoretical and computational modeling needed to link population activity to cognition and action.

  • Tagging, imaging & manipulating neural ensembles (optogenetics, DREADDs, 2-photon/multiphoton, miniscope imaging)
  • Theoretical neuroscience: computational modeling of population activity and behavior
Explore this area

Shared Infrastructure

Cross-Cutting Infrastructure

Both priority areas draw on the same shared investments in data, compute, and stimulation hardware, built to be useful across the whole cluster, not siloed to a single lab.

Affective Neuroimaging Consortium

ANIC is a data-sharing consortium spanning 54 collaborating labs worldwide and more than 3,000 participants. It's one of the most comprehensive functional-imaging datasets in existence, covering pain, pleasure, aversive stimuli, and food and drug cues.

Dual-H100 GPU Compute Node

Deployed in partnership with Dartmouth Research Computing, this shared GPU node gives cluster labs the large-scale computing power needed to train AI models that predict feeling states directly from neural data.

Multi-Technique Neurostimulation Facility

Inside the Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience Lab in Moore Hall, researchers combine TMS, tDCS, and Temporal Interference stimulation. Dartmouth is among the first universities worldwide with tTIS access, via the IT'IS Foundation's Early Adopter program.

These investments also feed Dartmouth's emerging, cross-campus integrated Neuroscience Institute initiative, translating neuroscience research into brain-disorder treatments, from fMRI-guided neurostimulation to clinical neuromodulation for epilepsy and serious mental illness.

Home / Research / Human Computation & Behavior

Priority Area 01

Human Computation and Behavior

Human neuroimaging (particularly fMRI and MEG) offers a unique window into human thought, experience, and behavior. This area asks what it takes to turn that window into a precise, quantitative science.

fMRI and MEG let researchers observe the living human brain as it thinks, feels, and decides, but raw signal alone doesn't explain behavior. This priority area is built around closing that gap: pairing human neuroimaging with the computational tools, data resources, and stimulation technologies needed to develop precise, quantitative models of the brain processes underlying feelings and cognitive performance, and to translate those models toward clinical use.

It draws together investigators across Psychological & Brain Sciences, Thayer School of Engineering, Geisel School of Medicine, and Dartmouth's Cognitive Science program, reflecting the cluster's broader mission to work across the traditional boundaries between those fields.

Sub-Focus Areas

Four ways this area is built

Pattern Recognition & Dynamic-Systems Models

Merging fMRI with pattern-recognition methods and dynamic-systems models of brain states, moving beyond static activation maps toward models of how brain states evolve over time.

Big-Data Resources & Large-Scale Computing

Leveraging large public resources (such as the UK Biobank's combined genetics, imaging, and health dataset) alongside large-scale computing to find patterns that no single-lab dataset could reveal.

Modeling Brain–Behavior Interrelationships

Advanced modeling of brain and behavioral data and how they relate to one another, including dynamic-systems approaches and network-topology models of brain organization.

Neuromodulation & Multimodal Recording

Combining neuroimaging with neuromodulation (TMS and tDCS) and multimodal brain recording such as simultaneous EEG and fMRI, to both measure and causally probe brain activity.

Current Activity

This area in action at Dartmouth

Not an abstract roadmap: active labs, real infrastructure, and work published this year.

Human brain stimulation program (Wager lab)

A collaboration hub with Thayer School of Engineering combining TMS, tDCS, and Temporal Interference stimulation. The program has already produced two papers in the journal Pain, and Dartmouth is among the first universities worldwide with Temporal Interference (tTIS) access, through the IT'IS Foundation's (Zurich) Early Adopter program.

Affective Neuroimaging Consortium (ANIC)

A data-sharing consortium of 54 collaborating labs worldwide and more than 3,000 participants. It's one of the most comprehensive functional-imaging datasets anywhere, covering pain, pleasure, aversive stimuli, and food and drug cues.

New dual-H100 GPU compute

Deployed with Dartmouth Research Computing, this shared compute node now powers AI models that aim to predict feeling states directly from neural data, a core near-term goal for the ANIC dataset.

Murray lab's first Dartmouth neuroimaging experiments

Building on 2024–2025 eye-tracking pilot work, the Murray lab is now running its first EEG and fMRI experiments at Dartmouth, testing models of attention and decision-making, in collaboration with Viola Stoermer of Psychological & Brain Sciences.

Home / Research / Neural Population Coding & Circuits

Priority Area 02

Neural Population Coding and Circuits

Modern neuroscience techniques are revolutionizing our understanding of neural circuits and how populations of neurons encode behavior. This area builds the tools, and the theory, to read that code directly.

Where fMRI and MEG reveal patterns across the whole human brain, this priority area works at the scale of individual neurons and the ensembles they form. New techniques for tagging, imaging, and manipulating neural populations, paired with theoretical models of how population-level activity gives rise to behavior, are opening a second, complementary window onto the same underlying question: how does neural activity encode mental states, decisions, and action?

This area is newer and smaller at Dartmouth than human neuroimaging, and it is deliberately being built out as one of the cluster's active priorities for growth.

Sub-Focus Areas

Two ways this area is built

Tagging, Imaging & Manipulating Neural Ensembles

New techniques for tagging, imaging, and manipulating neural ensembles tied to specific behavioral states, including optogenetics, DREADDs, functional tagging, 2-photon and multiphoton imaging, and miniscope-plus-GRIN-lens imaging in awake, behaving animals.

Theoretical Neuroscience

Computational modeling that links population-level neural ensemble activity to behavior, building the quantitative theory needed to interpret what large-scale recordings actually mean.

Current Activity

This area in action at Dartmouth

Centered today on the Murray lab's computational program and its external collaborations, with room built in to grow.

Computational modeling of neural circuits (Murray lab)

The Murray lab builds computational models of neural circuits and cognitive function, including working memory, thalamocortical organization, and brain-state dynamics, forming the theoretical core of this priority area at Dartmouth today.

Cortical microcircuitry & working-memory modeling

An ongoing collaboration with Yale, supported by an NSF center grant, developing models of how cortical microcircuits sustain working memory.

Credit assignment in reinforcement learning

A collaboration with Johns Hopkins, funded by an NIH R01, using monkey neuronal recordings to study how the brain assigns credit for outcomes during learning.

Autism & learning heterogeneity

A collaboration with UCLA Psychiatry, supported by a SFARI grant, studying heterogeneity in learning processes relevant to autism.

A growing area, and an active search

Neural population coding and circuits research is newer at Dartmouth than the cluster's human-neuroimaging work, and it is a deliberate growth priority. The cluster is actively searching for a third endowed faculty member whose work will bridge computational and systems neuroscience, further strengthening ties between human neuroimaging and animal-model circuit research.

    Cluster Timeline

    Past & Upcoming Events

    This timeline draws from the cluster's recent activity (publications, infrastructure, and public talks) and from what's ahead. It starts with what's coming next, then traces the record back to the cluster's earliest years.

    What's Next

    On the Horizon

    Directions the cluster is actively pursuing. Dates aren't fixed, so each entry is framed as a near-term goal rather than a firm calendar date.

    2026–2027Upcoming

    A New Clinical Trial for Cancer Pain

    Through the Dartmouth Innovation Accelerator for Cancer, the team is translating its tDCS neurostimulation advances into a clinical trial for oncology patients living with cancer pain.

    2026–2027Upcoming

    Growing ANIC with GPU-Powered AI Models

    The Affective Neuroimaging Consortium (ANIC) continues to expand, and the cluster's new dual-H100 GPU compute node will power AI models aimed at predicting feeling states directly from neural data.

    Coming this yearUpcoming

    Murray Lab's First EEG + fMRI Experiments

    Building on the lab's 2026 eye-tracking pilot work, the Murray lab plans its first combined EEG and fMRI experiments at Dartmouth, testing models of attention and decision-making.

    OngoingUpcoming

    Searching for a Third Endowed Faculty Member

    The cluster is actively searching for a third endowed faculty member whose work will bridge computational and systems neuroscience, further strengthening ties between human neuroimaging and animal-model circuit research.

    2026–2027Upcoming

    Supporting a Campus-Wide Neuroscience Institute

    The cluster is lending its expertise to Dartmouth's emerging, cross-campus integrated Neuroscience Institute initiative, which aims to translate neuroscience research into treatments for brain disorders: from fMRI-guided neurostimulation to clinical neuromodulation for epilepsy and serious mental illness.

    The Record

    Past Events

    Publications and infrastructure milestones since the cluster's earliest years, most recent first.

    2026

    2026

    New Book: Elements of fMRI Imaging

    Tor Wager's book, Elements of fMRI Imaging, entered production at MIT Press.

    2026

    On the Road with President Beilock

    Tor Wager and undergraduate researcher Jason Davis were interviewed by Dartmouth President Sian Leah Beilock as part of her “On the Road” series, hosted by the Dartmouth Club of New York.

    2026

    New Findings on Brain Stimulation for Pain

    The human brain stimulation program, run in collaboration with Thayer School of Engineering, published two papers in the journal Pain. A related randomized clinical trial, under review at Science Translational Medicine, found that precentral gyrus stimulation produced substantial pain reductions.

    2026

    Dartmouth Gains Early Access to Temporal Interference Stimulation

    Dartmouth became one of the first universities worldwide with Temporal Interference stimulation (tTIS) access, through the IT’IS Foundation's (Zurich) Early Adopter program.

    2026

    Murray Lab's First Human Study at Dartmouth

    The Murray lab conducted its first human behavioral study at Dartmouth, using eye tracking to study reinforcement learning and attention allocation. A related NSF grant with Viola Stoermer (PBS), on attention in learning, was recommended for funding.

    2026

    24 Peer-Reviewed Papers So Far in 2026

    The Wager lab published 24 peer-reviewed papers in 2026 alone, among them the three publications below.

    2026

    Targeted Placebo Effects Mapped in Science

    A Science paper from the Wager lab identified targeted placebo effects in specific brainstem body sites, evidence that placebo responses are organized with far more anatomical precision than previously understood.

    2026

    Insula Mapped Across 540 Participants in Nature Communications

    A Nature Communications paper mapped the insula's functional organization using fMRI data from 540 participants across 36 cohorts, one of the largest studies of this brain region to date.

    2026

    A Meta-Analysis of Placebo Effects in Nature Communications

    A second Nature Communications paper presented a meta-analysis of placebo effects across studies, consolidating evidence on how and when placebo responses occur.

    2026

    Moore Hall Neurostimulation Facility Opens

    A new multi-technique neurostimulation facility (supporting TMS, tDCS, and Temporal Interference stimulation) opened inside the Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience Lab in Moore Hall.

    2026

    New Courses for a New Generation

    John Murray launched a new graduate course, “Neural Computation.” Tor Wager taught “Mind, Brain, and Health,” a culminating-experience course on brain–body medicine.

    2026

    Dual-H100 GPU Compute Node Deployed

    The cluster partnered with Dartmouth Research Computing to deploy a dual-H100 GPU compute node, expanding capacity for large-scale modeling of neural and behavioral data.

    2026

    Affective Neuroimaging Consortium Reaches 54 Labs Worldwide

    The Affective Neuroimaging Consortium (ANIC), which the cluster helps lead, has grown to 54 collaborating laboratories worldwide and more than 3,000 research participants. It's one of the most comprehensive functional-imaging datasets of its kind, spanning pain, pleasure, aversive stimuli, and food and drug cues.

    2025

    2025

    Five-Year Follow-Up Published in JAMA Psychiatry

    A five-year follow-up study on Pain Reprocessing Therapy for chronic back pain was published in JAMA Psychiatry, extending the lab's original 2021 trial.

    2023

    2023

    A Banner Year for Publications

    The Wager lab published 21 peer-reviewed papers in 2022, with 9 more out by mid-2023.

    2023

    First Neuroimaging Signature for Drug Craving

    The lab published the first neuroimaging-based signature for drug craving, an objective marker of the neural patterns underlying persistent drug use and relapse risk.

    2023

    Large Trial Nearly Eliminates Chronic Back Pain

    In a large clinical trial, a four-week psychological and behavioral treatment eliminated or nearly eliminated chronic back pain in roughly two-thirds of patients, with gains maintained at one-year follow-up.

    2023

    The Most Comprehensive Analysis of Placebo Mechanisms to Date

    The lab published its most comprehensive analysis yet of the brain mechanisms behind placebo effects in pain, showing that placebos engage active healing processes.

    2021

    2021

    15 Papers in Neuron, Nature Communications, and More

    The Wager lab published 15 peer-reviewed papers in journals including Neuron, Nature Communications, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, Nature Medicine, and JAMA Psychiatry.

    2021

    A Landmark 150-Patient Pain Trial

    In a landmark chronic-pain clinical trial of 150 patients, a novel psychological and behavioral treatment eliminated or nearly eliminated pain in about 75% of participants, with gains lasting a year or more.

    2021

    tDCS Arrives at Dartmouth

    The Wager lab brought Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) to Dartmouth, in collaboration with Thayer School of Engineering.

    2021

    Faculty Search Launched

    The cluster launched an active search for an additional tenured or tenure-track professor and a staff research scientist, to expand its computational capacity.
